auth.notes: Every request is a JSON POST carrying AccountId and CognitoToken in the body, plus a fixed HTTP Basic Authorization header and a user agent that the app embeds (the same for every install; not reproduced here). The password is RSA-encrypted (PKCS#1 v1.5) with a public key embedded in the app and sent base64 as EncPassword. The client sends a MobileId it generates (an uppercase UUID) and should keep: a new MobileId looks like a new phone and triggers an emailed MFA code. The token lasts about a day and no refresh token is issued. Each login also counts against a per-account device binding limit.

data_leaves_device: Live and recorded video and audio used for alerts and clips (cloud-side classification of barking, crying, person, smoke alarm and pet activity)
Owner labels on the app's detections (training feedback)
The phone's latitude and longitude, written to the camera at setup
Wi-Fi network name, time zone and country
Device logs, on request (an upload-logs opcode exists)

endpoints.name: Login
endpoints.returns: AccountId and CognitoToken, or result code 12101 with an MfaAuthCodeCandidate when an emailed code is needed. A stored MfaAuthCode from an earlier verification skips the challenge.

endpoints.name: Send MFA code
endpoints.returns: Emails a code to the account; may return a refreshed MfaAuthCodeCandidate.

endpoints.name: Verify MFA code
endpoints.returns: MfaAuthCode, a proof to present on this and later logins.

endpoints.name: Device list
endpoints.returns: DeviceList[]: Id, DeviceName, ProductId, FirmwareVersion, DeviceStatus, P2PVendor, P2PUuid, DeviceToken, and P2PAccessToken on legacy cameras.

endpoints.name: P2P credential
endpoints.notes: The only cloud call a local P2P client strictly needs once it has the device list. Fetch it just before connecting, once, and share the session.
endpoints.returns: AuthKey (8 characters), P2PAccountId and a freshly issued P2PAccountKey for one DeviceId; all three null for a legacy camera. Every call invalidates the previously issued key.

cloud.failure_mode: Without the cloud a client cannot obtain a P2P credential, so it cannot open a session, and a camera cannot be set up. Whether a session opened with an earlier credential survives, or can be reopened, while the cloud is unreachable is not established. Alerts, clips, captions, summaries and the Nanny features stop outright.
cloud.notes: Only the credential path is documented here. The rest of the cloud API (alerts, subscriptions, events, the cloud treat toss) is out of scope; ha-furbo's furbo_cloud.py covers it. Result codes seen by ha-furbo: 12002 token rejected (also the answer to a wrong email or password at login), 12101 MFA required, 12102 wrong code, 12103 expired code, 80001 too many attempts, 80002 rate limited (TimeWait seconds in the body).

auth_params.notes: The token is issued by the vendor's login endpoint and sent in the JSON body of every request with the AccountId, not as an Authorization header. See cloud.auth and protocol_details.cloud_credential.

methods.notes: The only way to learn a camera's P2P UID and to get the credential a session needs. Each DeviceList entry also carries ProductId (which opcode set it speaks, see device.variants), FirmwareVersion, P2PVendor, DeviceToken and, on legacy cameras, P2PAccessToken. Reported by ha-furbo (verified on its FB0030 account).

TUTK LAN search: the SDK broadcasts a scrambled connect-by-UID probe and a camera on the same subnet answers, which is what makes a session come up in LAN mode. Port 32761 is the TUTK device listening port go2rtc's pure-Go client defaults to; that a Furbo listens there is a hypothesis. The probe and reply formats are go2rtc's (pkg/tutk/session0.go), not reproduced here, and the reply identifies a camera only by its P2P UID, so the cloud list is still needed to name it.

Finds a camera in setup mode only (the status light blinking yellow on the 360 and Mini models, green on the original Furbo). The regex is a slightly looser form of the app's rules, which are spelled out in device.identification.notes. Whether a provisioned camera keeps advertising is unknown.

identification.notes: No OUI is known for these cameras and none is claimed. Over BLE a setup-mode camera is recognised by its advertised name (see the ble_scan discovery method and device.variants); the app's exact rules are substring and prefix tests with length limits: contains 'Furbo3' and shorter than 12 characters, contains 'Furbo3C' and shorter than 14, contains 'Furbo4' and shorter than 12, contains 'MINICAM', starts with 'M2-', 'M3-' or 'M4-' and shorter than 12, starts with 'F2' and shorter than 5. A name containing 'Furbo' and shorter than 8 is treated as a first-generation unit the app cannot set up this way. A name containing '-S3' selects the current-generation GATT set, one containing 'FW3' the second older controller, anything else the first. The app then reads a 12-character device id out of the raw advertisement bytes, decoded as text with everything but letters, digits and '-' removed: the last 12 characters for the Furbo3/Furbo3C/Furbo4/M2/M3/M4 names, the first 12 otherwise. On the LAN nothing identifies a Furbo except a TUTK session to its UID.

device.name: Furbo Dog Camera (Furbo 2 / 2.5T, Furbo 360, Furbo Mini)
device.notes:
A Wi-Fi pet camera with a pan motor (on the 360 models), two-way audio and a treat launcher, sold with an optional Furbo Nanny subscription for cloud alerts, clips and summaries. Three surfaces, each documented here to the depth the evidence allows.
LOCAL CONTROL IS TUTK P2P, NOT RTSP. Every live path (video, microphone, talkback, state, settings, pan and treat toss) runs over one ThroughTek TUTK/Kalay P2P session: an IOTC session addressed by the camera's 20 character P2P UID, an AV channel inside it authenticated with a cloud-issued credential, and vendor IOCTRL messages on that channel. The SDK finds the camera by UDP broadcast, so a LAN-mode session needs the client on the camera's subnet; there is no connect-by-IP. Otherwise the session goes direct P2P through NAT, or through a Kalay relay (slow; video may not start). The session layout, both opcode sets and the A/V formats are in protocol_details. The schema has no transport for TUTK IOCTRL, so none of it is an executable `commands` block and the spec is identify_only until one exists (see evidence.open_questions).
FRESH CREDENTIALS NORMALLY COME FROM THE CLOUD. A client logs in to the Furbo cloud (email, RSA-encrypted password, and an emailed MFA code on first login from a new client id), lists the account's cameras, then asks for a P2P credential per camera. The key part is reissued on every fetch and the previous one stops working, so two clients (or the vendor app and a bridge) fetching independently lock each other out of the AV channel. Owner-exported account data and on-camera state are two credible recovery sources for a preserved credential. Whether one keeps working with both the vendor cloud and TUTK relays unavailable is still unproven. The flow is in cloud.endpoints and protocol_details.cloud_credential.
ONBOARDING IS BLE, AND IT REGISTERS THE CAMERA WITH THE CLOUD. A setup-mode camera advertises over BLE; the app reads a status code, triggers a Wi-Fi scan, reads the AP list back, writes the SSID and passphrase, then writes the account, a cloud endpoint and a short-lived registration token so the camera can register itself, then time zone, country, speaker volume and the phone's latitude and longitude. The current-generation GATT set is in protocol_details.ble_onboarding_v4 (its service UUID is not established, so it is not a `services` entry); the older generations' JSON channel is the 77f9a069-2ff9-4ff9-93b7-4db9689f4b53 service below. Everything here is from the app, not replayed.
TREAT TOSS IS A PHYSICAL ACTUATOR WITH A CONSUMABLE BEHIND IT. The app tosses one treat per button press (sometimes preceded by the treat-call sound). This spec documents only that. Repeated or scripted dispensing can overfeed a pet and fling treats hard enough to startle it; any automation should rate-limit itself and keep a person in the loop. The cloud treat-toss call answers success for any action string (ha-furbo's negative finding), so it proves nothing and is not documented further.
PRIVACY. This is an always-on camera and microphone in a home. Alerts (barking, crying, person, smoke alarm, pet activity), clips, captions and daily summaries are cloud features: the audio and video the classification runs on leave the house, and the app asks the owner to label its detections, which trains the vendor's models. At setup the app also writes the phone's latitude and longitude to the camera. A replacement client should be plain with its user about what it streams and where.
RTSP IS MODEL-SPECIFIC. Somerset Recon established (2021) that the older Furbo 2 served RTSP on TCP 554 at /stream, first unauthenticated and later with HTTP Digest authentication. The current app exposes no RTSP or ONVIF integration, and the same researcher found no listening service on the Furbo Mini. No current-model RTSP surface is established, so no camera block is declared. RTSP credentials are distinct from TUTK credentials.

openness.notes: Tomofun publishes no local API. The P2P transport is ThroughTek's proprietary TUTK/Kalay SDK, which the vendor licenses per app; the opcode set, the cloud credential flow and the BLE onboarding were all recovered by observation, by ha-furbo and by our own app analysis.

exclusivity.recovery: Nothing bonds, so there is nothing to forget in the phone's Bluetooth settings. The exclusivity that bites is on the P2P side: one cloud fetch of the P2P credential invalidates the key every other client holds, so the vendor app and a bridge fetching independently knock each other off (-20011 on the AV channel). Share one session.

pairing.notes: From the app: no bond is ever created, no MTU is requested, and every characteristic is used on a bare connection. Ownership is enforced by the cloud binding and the P2P credential, not by the radio link. Not checked on hardware.

unpair.clears: The cloud account binding, via 'Remove Device' in the app. There is no BLE bond to clear.

safety_advisory.detail: Each toss fires one treat across the room. Use it the way the vendor app does, one deliberate press at a time with the live view open. Automations that toss on a schedule or on an event should rate-limit themselves and keep a person watching; a jammed or empty hopper is not reported reliably enough (see the treat troubleshoot opcodes in protocol_details) to trust an unattended loop. This project is unaffiliated with Tomofun and the vendor's own instructions govern.
safety_advisory.summary: The treat launcher dispenses real food; scripted or repeated tossing can overfeed a pet.

security_advisory.detail: Somerset Recon published three write-ups (2021-2022). Furbo 2 (Ambarella S2Lm): a stack overflow in the RTSP server's digest authentication parser gave unauthenticated root code execution from the LAN (CVE-2020-24918; Ambarella's position is that the RTSP library was demo-only). Furbo 2.5T: command injection as root in a CGI program behind the camera's lighttpd server, which Somerset Recon labelled CVE-2021-32452 (no published CVE record exists as of 2026-09). Furbo Mini (Augentix SoC): firmware images fetched from a listable storage bucket, with no signature check and no TLS certificate verification on the download, so a network attacker could install modified firmware; reported unpatched in December 2022. None of this has been checked by this project, and the Furbo 360 (FB0030) is not named in any of it. Keep the camera on current firmware and on a network segment you trust.
security_advisory.summary: Published root exploits against older Furbo models; patch status unknown.

issued_to_client: Nothing locally. A P2P credential (the camera's UID, an 8-character AuthKey, a P2P account id and a P2P account key) is issued by the cloud on each request, and each request invalidates the previous key.
credentials.notes: On the current-generation set the passphrase, the account value, the registration token and the Wi-Fi-change proof travel AES-256-CBC encrypted under a key and IV that are constants in the app, the same for every install. That hides them from a casual BLE sniffer and from nobody who has the app; the BLE link itself is unencrypted and unpaired. A plain-hex passphrase characteristic also exists, used by the app only when the encrypted one is absent. The key and IV are not published here; an implementer extracts them from their own copy of the app. The older generations pass the whole JSON request through a transform in the app's native library, not analysed here.
stored_on_device: Cloud registration (account, endpoint; the registration token is short-lived)
Time zone, country code, the phone's latitude and longitude at setup, speaker volume

factory_reset.description: Procedures from Furbo's help centre, per model; none has been run by this project. The vendor's own articles disagree on the Furbo 360 hold time (5-10 s in the hard-reset article, 30 s in a setup article), so hold until the light changes rather than counting. The vendor also warns not to press reset just to change Wi-Fi networks; that is an in-app flow (see rejoin). The P2P opcode set has a remote reset request as well (protocol_details, marked advanced); the app's use of it was not traced.
factory_reset.effect: Disconnects the camera from Wi-Fi, forgets the network and puts it back in setup mode. It does not unbind the camera from its cloud account: the vendor says to also remove it from the account in the app, or the next setup fails.

procedures.basis: Furbo help centre, 'Hard Reset Your Furbo' (Furbo 360 Dog and Cat Camera articles) and 'Issues with Furbo Light Indicator'.
procedures.indicator: The status light starts blinking yellow (setup mode).
procedures.name: Furbo 360 and Furbo 360 Cat: reset button under the camera

steps.action: With the camera plugged in, press and hold the reset button underneath it for about 5 to 10 seconds.
Remove the camera from the old account in the Furbo app before setting it up again.

procedures.basis: Furbo help centre, 'Hard reset your Furbo' (original Furbo Dog Camera article).
procedures.indicator: The light changes colour, then turns green (setup mode).
procedures.name: Original Furbo (Furbo 2 / 2.5T): pinhole on the back, about 20 seconds

steps.action: With the camera plugged in, press and hold the pinhole reset button on the back with a pin or straightened paper clip for about 20 seconds, until the light changes colour.
Wait until the light turns green.

procedures.basis: Furbo help centre, 'Hard Reset Your Furbo Mini and Furbo Mini 360°'.
procedures.name: Furbo Mini (non-rotating): pinhole, 5-10 seconds

steps.action: With the camera plugged in, use a pin to press and hold the reset button for 5 to 10 seconds.

procedures.basis: Furbo help centre, 'Hard Reset Your Furbo Mini and Furbo Mini 360°', which gives no hold time.
procedures.name: Furbo Mini 360 (rotating): button under the device

steps.action: With the camera plugged in, press and hold the reset button underneath until the light starts blinking yellow.

ble.protocol: Furbo BLE setup, current generation (ASCII values on per-field characteristics)

cloud.local_alternative: None known. The camera requests registration data after joining Wi-Fi, and that data (a short-lived token and an endpoint) comes from the vendor cloud through the app.

methods.description: The flow the app runs for cameras whose advertised name contains '-S3'. Every value on the wire is ASCII text written with response; the device reports progress as an ASCII status code on a read/indicate characteristic and the app reacts to each code as it arrives. The characteristic table is protocol_details.ble_onboarding_v4 and the status codes are payload_formats.Status below. The characteristics are matched by UUID across all services, because which service holds them is not established. No bonding and no MTU request; indications are enabled by writing 0x0200 to each CCCD.
methods.name: Vendor app over Bluetooth (current-generation GATT set)

ApList.description: The Wi-Fi scan result, split across up to four read characteristics. The concatenated chunks form a JSON array; the app wraps it as {"ap_list": <array>} before parsing. Keys have a long and a one-letter spelling.

fields.description: SSID as lowercase hex of its UTF-8 bytes (also spelled 'n'). The app hex-decodes it, falling back to the raw text when it is not valid hex.
fields.name: name

fields.description: Security mode as a string (also spelled 'm'). Its vocabulary is not recorded.
fields.name: mode

fields.description: Signal strength, an integer (also spelled 's'). Whether it is dBm or a percentage is not recorded.
fields.name: signal

parse_rules: Read chunk 1, then 2, 3, 4, appending each; stop after a chunk that is empty or contains ']'.
Parse the concatenation as a JSON array of objects.
Hex-decode each name; show the list sorted and de-duplicated, as the app does.

Status.description: The status characteristic's value: an ASCII signed decimal integer, read and indicated. Codes are the device's; the labels are ours. The order in which a healthy setup walks them is inferred from the codes the app waits for and is not verified.
parse_rules: Decode the value as ASCII and parse a signed integer.
On the first read of a connection, a value below 0 or above 4 means a stale setup: restart it through the reset-setup characteristic before going on.
The app sorts failures three ways: -1 is a passphrase problem; -2, -3, -4, -8, -20 and -21 are router or internet problems; -30 and anything unlisted is a camera problem.

values.-101: Wi-Fi change requested but no ownership proof was written
values.-2: could not join the access point (read Wi-Fi mode and Wi-Fi error for detail)

steps.action: Plug the camera in and wait for setup mode: blinking yellow on Furbo 360 and Mini models, green on the original Furbo. Hard reset if it does not appear.
Scan for a name matching the ble_scan rule, take the 12-character device id from the advertisement, and connect. The app also checks with the cloud that the id is not bound to another account.
Enable indications on the status characteristic 02435612-dc14-423f-bd4f-a6a12e567e90 and read it.
steps.expect: An ASCII status code; '2' (advertising) or '4' (waiting for Wi-Fi details) means the camera is ready.

steps.action: If the first status read is negative or above 4, restart the camera's setup: write '0' to fb6dfec1-257c-4d58-9eed-6f79599919f0 (registration-ready flag off), enable indications on 2c259f9c-4a57-4c74-830e-2013e4466c2c and write '1' to it ('2' when re-pointing an already bound camera, see rejoin). Wait for it to indicate '0', then refresh the GATT cache and rediscover services.
Enable indications on the scan-ready characteristic 3c2c5dea-35aa-4540-94be-0bd5d9e72793 and read it. If it is not '1', write '0' to it to start a Wi-Fi scan and wait for it to indicate '1'.

Read the AP list chunks e92543cb-08c6-4b2b-a395-1824cdbd4417, a43251f9-1d8c-41d0-9804-879b992d4748, 325d3a42-5102-4c55-aad6-20c7b1157997, 76e415d0-9e94-4979-aaa2-54d8489f7456 in order, stopping after the first chunk that is empty or contains ']'. Concatenate them and parse as payload_formats.ApList. If fewer than six characters came back, rescan (the app retries twice).
Pick the 2.4 GHz network and enter its passphrase, or type a hidden SSID by hand.

Write the SSID as lowercase hex of its UTF-8 bytes to 233d5fb2-f565-4fef-832a-983d6c362f36. Write the passphrase: if f72deed1-3198-4df6-b0d7-e472cea7885f exists, its encrypted form there (see protocol_details.ble_onboarding_v4.field_encryption), otherwise its lowercase hex to ac075b73-2424-4e7a-9fe2-62cbf19e7e89. Then write '1' to 2474cee2-379d-4a0c-b630-37dd53965ca2.
steps.expect: The status moves to 8 (joining the AP), then 9, 10 and 12.

steps.action: The camera joins Wi-Fi, takes a DHCP lease, checks DNS and checks that the cloud is reachable.

On status 20, write the registration data: the account value (encrypted to cb04b5ee-4c79-4316-a50e-8cc4a2067840 if present, else plain to 3c1a8fd9-ac74-4062-80cc-b2947cb7a039), the cloud endpoint to 81f6f485-eae6-41cc-8a2f-e11a5844a114, the short-lived registration token (encrypted to e42de30f-a772-43fe-b216-ca5b78db4d82 if present, else plain to 953b64d3-99bd-4434-b050-1c39512f9f95), then '1' to fb6dfec1-257c-4d58-9eed-6f79599919f0. Enable indications on f60a6339-0647-42a4-b709-29a3e620c0af and 41f21774-cc72-44f2-a002-86bdbedc253d for the camera's HTTP and service error codes.
The camera registers itself with the vendor cloud (status 13, then 14).

On status 21, write the settings: longitude to 00002aaf-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and latitude to 00002aae-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (ASCII decimal, seven fractional digits), the two-letter country code to f34375ad-c23c-4bb5-bbfe-13d624741757, '60' to the speaker volume 1a19aaae-094a-47aa-aaa3-1d66bd08ab1a, the IANA time zone name plus a trailing 0x00 to 00002a0e-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, then '1' to 3c2fb8ce-49b9-4e1c-848f-8a26740e7c8c.
The camera applies the settings (22), starts its P2P service (15) and reports '0' when a P2P session is possible. The app then opens a P2P session and asks for a camera name.
steps.expect: Status '0'. If it stays at 15 for 20 s the app treats setup as done anyway.

timing.notes: The app's own timeouts, each armed when the named status first arrives and cleared when the status changes. A repeated status does not re-arm its timer.

causes: The camera is not in setup mode. Hard reset until the light blinks yellow (green on the original Furbo).
Phone Bluetooth is off or wedged. The vendor's advice is to toggle Bluetooth, restart the phone, and unplug and replug the camera.
A first-generation camera: a name containing 'Furbo' and shorter than 8 characters is refused by this app's BLE flow.
troubleshooting.symptom: The app cannot find the camera ('can't connect to your Furbo')

causes: The scan-ready characteristic never indicated '1' within 70 s. Write '0' again; the app retries twice.
troubleshooting.symptom: Wi-Fi scan never completes (the app's 'scan timeout')

causes: A chunk read failed, or the concatenation is not valid JSON. The app re-reads from chunk 1 after a rescan.
troubleshooting.symptom: The AP list cannot be read or parsed

causes: It is 5 GHz only. Furbo joins 2.4 GHz only.
It is hidden. Enter the SSID by hand.
Weak signal. The vendor suggests setting up within about 1.5 m of the router.
troubleshooting.symptom: My network is not in the list

causes: Wrong passphrase, or a WPA3-only network. The vendor says WPA3 is not supported; switch the router to WPA2 or WPA2/WPA3 mixed.
troubleshooting.symptom: Status -1 or -2 after the credentials are written

causes: It is still bound to an account. After a hard reset, remove the camera from the old account in the app, then set it up again.
troubleshooting.symptom: Setup fails for a camera that was set up before

ble.protocol: Furbo BLE setup, older generations (JSON over one write and one notify characteristic)

methods.description: For cameras whose advertised name does not contain '-S3' (the Furbo 2 generation and the first Mini, by the app's name rules; which hardware that is exactly is unverified). One service, 77f9a069-2ff9-4ff9-93b7-4db9689f4b53, with a write characteristic 026048ab-fafc-48e5-9db0-a9bc46368055 and a notify/indicate characteristic 30c95538-58f8-4db4-a62e-08af4bae4cb0. Requests are JSON objects {"c": "<4-digit command>", "d": {...}} (one app revision adds a fixed ten-character placeholder in "s"); '0001' asks for the AP list, '0002' sends the Wi-Fi and registration details (device_id, ssid, password, accesstoken, user, endpoint). A later revision (names containing 'FW3') adds '0022' and '0023'. Both revisions pass the JSON through a transform in the app's native library before writing it as base64 text, which this project has not analysed, so the bytes cannot be reproduced from this spec. After each write the app writes 'ENM' without response as an end marker; replies arrive as notifications, accumulated until one equal to 'ENM', then decoded the same way. See protocol_details.ble_onboarding_legacy.
methods.name: Vendor app over Bluetooth (older-generation JSON channel)

steps.action: Put the camera in setup mode and connect to service 77f9a069-2ff9-4ff9-93b7-4db9689f4b53.
Enable notifications (or indications, whichever the characteristic offers) on 30c95538-58f8-4db4-a62e-08af4bae4cb0.
Send command '0001' with the 12-character device id; the reply's data carries the AP list.
Send command '0002' with the device id, SSID, passphrase, access token, user and endpoint; a reply result of 0 is success.

timing.notes: App timeouts: 60 s for the AP list, 100 s for the set-Wi-Fi reply in the first revision and 10 s in the later one.

setup.notes: Setup is the vendor app over BLE, and it is not only a Wi-Fi handover: after joining the network the camera asks for registration data (the account, a cloud endpoint and a short-lived token the app fetches from the cloud) and registers itself with the vendor cloud before it reports success. Everything below is from static analysis of the app; nothing has been replayed, and whether a camera ever completes setup without the cloud is unknown. The network must be 2.4 GHz and WPA2 (the vendor states that 5 GHz and WPA3 do not work); a hidden SSID is typed in by hand. The survey behind this spec reports that newer "Subscription Required" units need a paid plan at setup, and the app does have a licence step that can fail; neither is verified.

rejoin.notes: The app's 'Reset Wi-Fi' menu item re-runs the BLE flow on a bound camera without a hard reset (the vendor says the light shows blinking blue when the camera has lost its network). In the current-generation set the app writes '2' instead of '1' to the reset-setup characteristic and, with the new credentials, writes an ownership proof it holds for that camera, encrypted, to d6f178c9-8137-4d18-8ced-0b62d7e3e7f2; a missing or wrong proof ends with status -101 or -102. Where the app gets that proof was not traced. P2P sessions need no change afterwards: the UID is the camera's, not the network's.

steps.action: Plug the camera in near the new router (blinking blue light when it cannot reach its old network).
In the vendor app choose the camera, then 'Reset Wi-Fi', and let the phone connect over Bluetooth.

Write '2' to 2c259f9c-4a57-4c74-830e-2013e4466c2c, then run the scan and credential steps of the primary method, adding the encrypted ownership proof to d6f178c9-8137-4d18-8ced-0b62d7e3e7f2 before the ready flag.

testing.notes: Nobody on this project has driven a Furbo from this document, and the research store holds no capture and no firmware. The P2P session, the V3 opcode set, pan, one treat toss, H.264 at 1920x1080 and G.711 talkback frames were verified on real hardware (an FB0030 on firmware 108, TUTK library 003.011, 2026-09-05) by the ha-furbo project, per its HARDWARE_VERIFICATION.md; the legacy (FB002) credential path was verified by a contributor in ha-furbo issue 3. That is third-party evidence, recorded per fact as `reported`. The BLE onboarding surface comes from static analysis of the vendor app only.

variants.name: Furbo Dog Camera, first generation (hypothesis)
variants.notes: Cloud ProductId FB001 speaks the V2 opcode set per ha-furbo. Which product it is and how it advertises are not established; a BLE name containing 'Furbo' and shorter than 8 characters is what the app treats as first generation and refuses.

variants.name: Furbo Dog Camera 2 (hypothesis)

The cloud issues it no AuthKey, P2PAccountId or P2PAccountKey; it authenticates with the account id and the device record's P2PAccessToken in the clear (ha-furbo issue 3, verified on FB002 hardware by a contributor). The 'F2' BLE prefix mapping is a hypothesis from the app's name rules. Somerset Recon's RTSP and root exploit reports concern this generation.

variants.notes: V2 opcode set per ha-furbo. The FCC label exhibit reads MODEL Furbo2.5T, 5 V 2 A input. That the label model and cloud ProductId FB0025 are the same product is a hypothesis. BLE name rule not established (possibly 'F2', like the Furbo 2).

variants.notes: V3 opcode set. The one model the P2P half of this spec was verified on (ha-furbo, firmware 108). The link from ProductId FB0030 to the sticker model 'Furbo3' and the BLE name 'Furbo3...' is by the vendor's model table and the app's setup types, not observed.

variants.notes: V3 opcode set per ha-furbo. Product not identified; possibly what the app's 'Furbo4' setup type covers.

variants.name: Furbo 360 Cat Camera (sticker model 'FurboCat', hypothesis)

evidence.app_static_analysis: The vendor Android app 7.83.1 was decompiled and read for facts only. Its current-generation BLE setup controller gave every characteristic UUID above, the role of each (from its use sites and log labels), the ASCII value conventions, the status-code table, the per-status timeouts, the chunked AP list and its JSON keys, and the fixed-key AES-256-CBC wrapping of four fields. Its two older controllers gave the 77f9a069-2ff9-4ff9-93b7-4db9689f4b53 service, the JSON command envelope, the 'ENM' end marker and two result tables. Its BLE manager gave the advertised-name rules and the 12-character device id extraction. Its P2P command layer (one implementation per opcode set) confirmed the V3 opcode numbers ha-furbo publishes, the toss and pan request payloads and the app's 60/50 degree pan step. RESEARCH.md's first pass called the camera cloud-only; the app in fact carries the ThroughTek TUTK SDK, and the local P2P path is ha-furbo's finding. Nothing was replayed.

evidence.open_questions: See remaining_unknowns. First things to settle with a camera in hand: whether a session opened with a stored credential works with the WAN cut; whether the camera finishes BLE setup without registering; which service holds the current-generation characteristics; what the microphone codec 135 is. For the schema: a TUTK/IOCTRL transport (a command addressed by a 32-bit opcode on a session's AV channel, with a payload template and a reply keyed by opcode plus one) would let the V3 table become executable `commands` and `entities`; proposed in the return notes of this change rather than in spec-evolution.md.
evidence.open_source_review: willbeeching/ha-furbo at b2a65be1 (MIT): furbo_p2p.py (session order, both opcode tables, reply decoding, talkback header, legacy path), furbo_cloud.py (credential flow, result codes), furbo_bridge.py (value ranges its API enforces), DOCS.md (single-session rule, LAN mode, relay, token lifetime) and HARDWARE_VERIFICATION.md (what was run on the FB0030, including the negative cloud treat-toss finding). ha-furbo derives from its own decompile of the app, so its agreement with ours on opcode numbers is two readings of one source, not independent confirmation. enter.notes: The app can ask a camera to update over P2P (an upgrade request in each opcode set, listed as advanced in protocol_details and deliberately not documented further), and the version fields of the upgrade-info reply say whether one is pending. How the camera then finds and applies the image is not known.

image.notes: The camera fetches its own image. Somerset Recon reported (2022) that the Furbo Mini's SWU images carried no signature and were downloaded without TLS certificate verification; other models are not covered by that report and nothing here is verified.

dfu.notes: OTA is outside this spec's scope. This block exists so a consumer never offers an update path it cannot see, and so the upgrade and reset opcodes stay behind the advanced flag.

recovery.notes: Somerset Recon describes A/B boot slots on the Mini, which would keep the old image; unverified and unknown for other models.

covers: Live H.264 video (1080p or 360p on the FB0030)
Microphone audio and G.711 u-law talkback
Camera on/off, speaker volume, night vision, barking sensitivity, auto tracking and zoom, voice control, treat size
not_covered: Setup and Wi-Fi changes (BLE flow that registers with the cloud)
Alerts, clips, captions, daily summaries, Nanny features
local_access.notes: The TUTK SDK is proprietary and licensed per app; ha-furbo builds against a copy fetched at build time and ships none. go2rtc's pure-Go TUTK package is the SDK-free route, but whether it handles the Furbo's DTLS AV channel with the account/key identity is not established.
local_access.summary: The camera speaks TUTK P2P on the LAN as shipped, and a same-subnet client reaches it in LAN mode with no traffic leaving the house for the session itself. But the credential for that session comes from the vendor cloud, freshly, each time.

microphone.format: Not established. The FB0030 labels its microphone frames with codec id 135, whose meaning lives in the TUTK library; ha-furbo tests each stream with a decoder instead of trusting the id.
microphone.start: Standard TUTK opcode 0x300 with int32 0; stop 0x301. Frames arrive on a separate queue from video.

talkback.format: G.711 u-law, 16 kHz, mono; 320-byte frames (20 ms), paced in real time.
talkback.frame_header: 16 bytes: codec id (int16 LE, 137 = G.711 u-law), flags (uint8: sample-rate index in bits 2-5 over 8000/11025/12000/16000/22050/24000/32000/44100/48000 Hz, bit 1 set for 16-bit, bit 0 set for stereo; 14 = 16 kHz, 16-bit, mono), camera index (uint8), online count (uint8), 7 reserved bytes, timestamp in ms (uint32 LE).
talkback.notes: Verified by ha-furbo at the P2P layer on the FB0030: the camera accepts frames. The talkback AV server uses security mode 3 while the client channel uses mode 1; the triage brief's 'security mode 3' is the talkback channel.
talkback.open: Get a free IOTC channel on the session, send standard opcode 0x350 (speaker start) with [channel as int32 LE, 4 x 0x00], then start an AV SERVER on that channel with security mode 3 (DTLS, PSK-AES128-CBC-SHA256) and authentication callbacks that accept everything, as the app does; set a resend buffer (ha-furbo uses 512 KiB, since a zero buffer rejects every frame). Close with 0x351 and the same payload, then stop the server and turn the channel off.

video.frames: Read with the SDK's frame call; the frame header carries codec id, key-frame flag, frame rate, a millisecond timestamp and the frame number.
video.observed_fb0030: Quality 0 gave H.264 1920x1080 at 25 fps after one 640x360 preview frame; qualities 1 to 3 all gave 640x360 (ha-furbo, HARDWARE_VERIFICATION.md). The FB0030 serves no 720p.
video.start: Standard TUTK opcode 0x1ff with a 4-byte little-endian int32 quality number; stop with 0x2ff. The camera answers 0x933.

commands.0001: Get the AP list. d: {device_id}. The reply's d carries the list (same item keys as the current set's ApList).
commands.0002: Set Wi-Fi and registration. d: {device_id, ssid, password, accesstoken, user, endpoint}. The first revision passes ssid and password through a text-escaping helper first.
commands.0022: Later revision only. d: {device_id}. Role not traced (polled during setup).
commands.0023: Later revision only, no data. Role not traced.

ble_onboarding_legacy.envelope: Request: a JSON object with "c" (a four-digit command code as a string) and "d" (an object); the first revision also sends "s" with a fixed ten-character placeholder. Reply: a JSON object with "r" (integer result, 0 success), "c" (the command it answers) and "d" (data), plus optional "e", "v", "f", "i", "dt", "md", "hc" (integer; by analogy with the current set an HTTP return code), "se" (integer; service error) and "we" (integer; Wi-Fi error). The other keys' roles are not recorded.
ble_onboarding_legacy.framing: The app writes the request (write with response), and on write success, if the value was not exactly three bytes, writes 'ENM' without response as an end marker. Replies are notifications appended together until one equals 'ENM'. Both revisions route the JSON through the app's native library, which returns base64 text on the way out and is applied in reverse on the way in; the transform was not analysed, so no byte-exact example exists.

ble_onboarding_v4.excluded_uuids: A naive UUID search of the app also finds identifiers of its analytics SDK (prefixes a029f440-, 46bad1ed-, 383f2407-, 8d9792b7-). They are not device UUIDs.
ble_onboarding_v4.field_encryption: AES-256-CBC with PKCS#7 padding. The key is 32 ASCII characters and the IV 16 ASCII characters, both constants in the app and identical for every install; they are not reproduced here. The ciphertext is sent as base64 without line breaks. For the passphrase the plaintext is its lowercase-hex string, not the passphrase itself; for the account, the token and the ownership proof it is the raw text. The app writes the encrypted form whenever the camera exposes the encrypted characteristic.
ble_onboarding_v4.notification_setup: The app enables indications (CCCD 0x0200), not notifications, on every characteristic it subscribes to.
ble_onboarding_v4.service_uuid: Not established. The app matches characteristics by UUID across all services. It also declares four vendor UUIDs it never references (7d7316ab-796b-46de-a6a3-b49d9779789e, 4ef3767f-1ff0-423a-98ca-aba79f75e0af, 923b0d97-2131-4d77-9ce9-56ff8998b4e9, 5650bad3-8798-437f-966e-a5c92c603fe3), which are probably the service UUIDs; a hypothesis.
ble_onboarding_v4.source: Static analysis of the vendor app's current-generation BLE setup controller (7.83.1).
ble_onboarding_v4.value_encoding: Every value is ASCII text. Writes are with response (Android write type default), UTF-8 bytes of the string, with no terminator except the time zone, which ends in one 0x00. A write with no value sends a single 0x00. Reads and indications decode as UTF-8.

offline_recovery.account_export: The UID, AuthKey, P2PAccountId and P2PAccountKey (or the legacy account/token pair) can be preserved by the owner. Public hardware research also documents on-camera p2p_auth.json state; deleting that state causes new credentials on the next cloud setup. These are owner-recovery sources, not credential-free adoption or a universal password.
offline_recovery.persistence: Expect credentials to survive reboot until reset, re-registration or regeneration. A same-LAN session with both the vendor cloud and TUTK relays unavailable still requires an owner-authorized capture. Furbo 2's RTSP Digest credential is a separate secret and cannot be derived from these TUTK fields.

cloud_credential.secrets: The UID, AuthKey, P2P account id and key, AccountId, CognitoToken, MfaAuthCode and DeviceToken are all per-owner secrets. An owner obtains their own through the login above; none belongs in a spec, a log or a bug report.
steps: POST /v5/account/read/login with Email, EncPassword, MobileId and, if the client has one, the MfaAuthCode from an earlier verification.

If the answer is result code 12101, POST /v4/account/mfa/login/send-code with the MfaAuthCodeCandidate, ask the owner for the emailed code, POST /v4/account/mfa/verify with it, then POST /v2/account/login with the resulting MfaAuthCode. Keep MfaAuthCode and MobileId for next time.
POST /v2/account/{AccountId}/device and pick the camera by Id; note P2PUuid, ProductId and, for legacy cameras, P2PAccessToken.

POST /v5/device/p2p_connection/get with the DeviceId. All three of AuthKey, P2PAccountId, P2PAccountKey present: modern path. All three null: legacy path. Anything in between: refuse rather than guess, as ha-furbo does.

ioctrl_framing.notifications: Unsolicited messages use their own opcodes (the 0x30000 range on V3) and are not replies.
ioctrl_framing.pacing: ha-furbo waits up to 0.4 s per reply on a V3 state sweep and moves on; on a LAN session replies arrive in milliseconds.
ioctrl_framing.rejection: A request the camera will not serve is answered with opcode 0x40001 and payload [status, opcode bits 0-7, opcode bits 8-15, 0, 0]. Only the low 16 bits of the refused opcode come back, so 0x10009 and 0x20009 look alike; match a refusal against the request that is outstanding.
ioctrl_framing.reply: The reply opcode is the request opcode plus one (a reply carrying the request opcode itself is also seen). The payload starts with a status byte, 0 meaning success, unless noted.
ioctrl_framing.request: One IOCTRL message on the AV channel: a 32-bit opcode and a payload. Most requests carry 4 bytes; unused bytes are 0x00.

ioctrl_v2.notes: The older opcode set, from ha-furbo's reading of the vendor app. Not hardware-verified beyond video and the legacy credential path on an FB002 (ha-furbo issue 3). Requests are 4 bytes unless noted. V2 has no pan.

tutk_session.lan_mode: LAN mode needs the client and camera in one broadcast domain. Across VLANs, allow UDP both ways between the two hosts (the session then comes up as direct P2P) or relay the search broadcast.
tutk_session.single_session_rule: One session per camera, shared by video, audio and control. Every cloud fetch reissues P2PAccountKey, so a second session (or the phone app) that fetches its own credential invalidates the first one's key; both then fail with -20011 and ha-furbo saw this wedge video and controls for hours.
tutk_session.source: ha-furbo furbo-bridge/src/furbo_p2p.py and DOCS.md; hardware-verified there on FB0030 firmware 108
steps: Initialise the SDK once per process: set the licence string the vendor app uses (an app-wide constant that the vendor SDK requires; not published here), initialise IOTC on a random local UDP port (the app uses 10000 plus the current time modulo 10000), then initialise AV. The app sets no region.
Fetch a P2P credential for the camera from the cloud (cloud.endpoints 'P2P credential') immediately before connecting.
Modern camera: connect by UID with authentication type 0 and the 8-character AuthKey. Legacy camera (the cloud returned no AuthKey): the plain parallel connect by UID with no key.
Check the session: mode 0 is direct P2P, 1 is relay, 2 is LAN. Relay makes commands slow and can stop video starting.

Start the AV client on IOTC channel 0: identity P2PAccountId, password P2PAccountKey, resend on, security mode 1 (DTLS, PSK-AES128-CBC-SHA256), auth type 0. Legacy camera: identity the account id, password the device record's P2PAccessToken, security mode 0 (no DTLS), auth type 0. ha-furbo raised the client receive buffers to 10 MiB.
V2 cameras only: send the account's DeviceToken, NUL-terminated, with the V2 set-device-token opcode. V3 cameras take nothing (the app's V3 implementation of that call sends nothing).
Before each IOCTRL send, drain anything already queued, so the command's own reply is not consumed by the drain.
Close: exit IOCTRL, stop the AV client, stop the connect and close the session. Deinitialise the SDK only at process exit.

remaining_unknowns: Whether a P2P session can be opened, or an open one survives, with the internet down, using a credential fetched earlier.
Which GATT service holds the current-generation setup characteristics, and the characteristics' declared property bits.
Whether a camera joins Wi-Fi and stays usable if the registration step (status 20) is never answered, i.e. whether any cloud-free setup exists.
The vocabularies of the Wi-Fi mode, Wi-Fi error, HTTP return code and service error characteristics, and of the AP list's mode field; whether signal is dBm or percent.
What the account value written during registration is (email or account id), and where the app's Wi-Fi-change ownership proof comes from.
The native transform the older BLE generations apply to their JSON, and the roles of commands '0022' and '0023' and the reply keys e, v, f, i, dt, md.
Which hardware maps to which ProductId, BLE name rule, GATT generation and opcode set: every variants entry except FB0030's opcode set is a hypothesis.
Behaviour without a Furbo Nanny subscription, and whether 'Subscription Required' units do anything before activation.
The microphone codec (FB0030 labels it 135) and whether it is the same on other models.
Whether go2rtc's SDK-free TUTK client can open the Furbo's DTLS AV channel with the P2P account/key identity.
Whether the camera listens on UDP 32761 for LAN connections, as TUTK devices usually do.
The reply layouts of get_time_zone, get_network_info and the treat troubleshoot opcodes, the payloads of set_treat_sound, set_auto_calm and play_auto_calm_audio on V3, and the notification payloads.
Somerset Recon's RTSP report on the Furbo 2 and its no-open-ports report on the Mini: neither checked here. No port scan of any model is in the research store.
Firmware update mechanics, signing and recovery on any model.
Whether a provisioned camera still advertises over BLE.

services.name: Device Information
services.notes: Read by the app during current-generation setup and reported with its analytics. Only the three characteristics below are used; their exact contents on each model are not recorded.

initialization.description: Open notifications (or indications) before the first request. The app picks the CCCD value from the characteristic's property bits; it sets the descriptor value but its older controllers never write the descriptor, so whether the camera notifies without a CCCD write is an open question. A client should write it.

services.name: Furbo setup service, older generations
services.notes: The service the app's two older setup controllers open by UUID. JSON requests go out on 026048ab-fafc-48e5-9db0-a9bc46368055 and replies come back on 30c95538-58f8-4db4-a62e-08af4bae4cb0, both through a native transform this project has not analysed (see the older-generation setup method and protocol_details.ble_onboarding_legacy). Properties are those the app uses; the device's declared property bits are not recorded.
